title: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault
description: Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a crimin
body: Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a criminal sexual act against a former assistant.In a victim-impact statement in court, Miriam Haley said the assault had had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away".Appearing in court in a wheelchair, Weinstein denied the allegations but apologised to "anyone I may have hurt by my actions". Weinstein has already spent several years jailed in New York, where he has faced three trials over rape and abuse allegations. He was convicted in a separate sex-crime case in Los Angeles. This is the second time he has been given a prison sentence in the Miriam Haley case. Weinstein was first convicted and sentenced in 2020, but New York's highest court overturned the conviction in 2024, along with another involving actress Jessica Mann. The court ruled that Weinstein did not get a fair trial.He was retried and convicted again last year on a single charge of a criminal sexual act against Haley.Weinstein, 74, is currently being held in a prison ward at New York's Bellevue Hospital for a series of ailments reported during his incarceration.Once the high-flying producer behind Miramax, the studio that produced hits like Shakespeare in Love, Weinstein fell from grace in 2017 after the New York Times and the New Yorker revealed multiple women's allegations of sexual assault stretching back decades. The accusations against him sparked the #MeToo movement, but New York prosecutors have had to navigate a twisting path in securing convictions and sentences.In the 2020 trial, Haley testified that Weinstein had assaulted her in a bedroom in his Manhattan apartment in 2006. Haley was a production assistant on the Project Runway television series at the time. On charges related to Mann, juries could not reach a verdict, and he was found not guilty in another charge involving model Kaja Sokola. After testifying in the retrial last year, Haley told the BBC she felt compelled to take the stand. "I just thought, I have to stand up for myself. I have to stand up for the truth," she said.Weinstein is still awaiting sentencing in California, where he was convicted in 2022 of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in a hotel room in 2013. An appeals court ordered he be re-sentenced in the case after the New York convictions were overturned.Weinstein has consistently denied the allegations against him, and said he believes he will be proven innocent.On Wednesday, Judge Curtis Farber criticised the former Hollywood mogul as he announced the 15-year sentence."You took what you wanted by force and you have never accepted responsibility," Farber said.

schema.headline: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault

title: Maricarmen: Eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage
description: The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's ho
body: The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's housing crisis.The tenant of the flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay the rent set by the investment firm that owns it.Maricarmen's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent. However, the company that bought the property in 2018, Urbagestión, cited a legal glitch allowing it to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650.It subsequently lowered the new rent to €1,650 but Maricarmen was still unable to pay it with her monthly pension of €1,350.Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention. Supporters of Maricarmen camped outside the building on Tuesday night, joined by celebrities including Javier Bardem's brother, Carlos, and the singer Ana Belén, who read out the poem Desahucio (Eviction) by Rafael Alberti.Several hundred people, mostly youngsters, had gathered by the morning in a bid to prevent the eviction from taking place, chanting "Maricarmen stays". Some activists blocked the stairs inside the building.In a video posted on social media, a tearful Maricarmen thanked those who had come out to support her against "this cruel struggle by someone who wants to earn money".The possibility of a last-minute reprieve for Maricarmen appeared when an anonymous donor offered to pay most of her rent. However, Urbagestión reportedly rejected the offer and the eviction went ahead."Today is a very sad day, a very dramatic day, when it's plain to see the effects of unbridled speculation, of not wanting to control the market, of putting out the red carpet for the vultures and the speculators," said Housing Minister Teresa Rodríguez.A shortage of available housing has been blamed for soaring rental costs in recent years, which have left millions of Spaniards struggling to find affordable homes. In Madrid, rentals have increased by more than 100% over the last decade, according to property site Idealista, with a 10% rise over the last year.The Socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has frequently targeted companies whose investment pushes up housing costs. In January, the prime minister said he aimed to "protect those who are most exposed to that speculation and that greed".However, some critics of the government say it needs to work harder to build new homes, and others warn that its rhetoric discourages many owners from placing their properties on the rental market.

schema.headline: Maricarmen: Eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage

title: 105-year-old investigated over murders at Nazi PoW camp in Germany
description: German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war c
body: German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war camp in World War Two.The suspect is alleged to have been a camp guard at Stalag 326 VI K in Senne in northwestern Germany.A similar case had also been under way involving a second former camp guard at Senne, Dortmund public prosecutor Sonja Frodermann said in a statement.That suspect died a few months ago at the age of 99, she said.No further details about the two former guards have been made public, however the two cases highlight the difficulties faced by prosecutors who continue to investigate Nazi-era crimes, with most of the remaining suspects already dead.More than 5.3 million soldiers from the Soviet Red Army were held in German captivity during World War Two and half are thought to have died. Many of those who did survive were treated as traitors on their return home.But the PoW camp, or Stalag, at Senne was one of the biggest.One in three Soviet PoWs entering Nazi Germany between 1941 and 1945 went through the complex at Senne, according to the memorial site, and they often ended up doing forced labour in the wider region. Living conditions at Stalag were horrific, and prisoners faced appalling mistreatment and malnutrition.Of the 180,000-200,000 Soviet prisoners of war registered there, many died and tens of thousands are buried there. PoWs from France, Poland, Serbia and Belgium were also held at Senne.

schema.headline: 105-year-old investigated over murders at Nazi PoW camp in Germany

title: Iran's president tells Trump it will never 'bend the knee'
description: "The US president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism," Iran's president told the UN in New York.He then held up a photo
body: "The US president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism," Iran's president told the UN in New York.He then held up a photo of the country's late Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in a strike on his residence when the US and Israel launched a joint attack in late February.He also presented pictures of some of the more than 175 civilians, two thirds of them children, who Iranian authorities say were killed in missile strikes on a primary school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd that day. The US has denied striking Lamerd and said it is still investigating what happened in Minab."Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed on our country. And we defended ourselves with utmost strength," Pezeshkian said.Also on Wednesday, an attack on a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz killed an Indian sailor, the Agence France-Presse news agency reported, citing Omani and Indian authorities. The attack was condemned by India's foreign ministry, which called for unimpeded passage through the Strait to be restored. In February, Iran retaliated for the massive US-Israeli air campaign by launching deadly missile and drone attacks on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases.It also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, by attacking commercial vessels in the Gulf, the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. The US responded by imposing a blockade of Iranian ports and ships in April.In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran wants to retain some measure of control over the strait and collect fees from vessels that use it, which the US has rejected.In his address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said he faced a "big decision" - either negotiate a deal that would allow Iranians to rebuild their country, or "annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly".Pezeshkian said the threat was "a sign of a bullying mentality"."[Trump] must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend the knee," he said.But he added: "We are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force."Pezeshkian made clear that the US blockade would have to end as part of any deal."It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access to shipping through this waterway," he said.He also reiterated that Iran would not give up its right to have a civilian nuclear programme and that it would not seek to develop nuclear weapons."We say it clearly: no nuclear weapons and no limitations on peaceful nuclear technology."Trump argued in his speech that the war had prevented Iran from obtaining a nuclear bomb and demanded that its leaders "relinquish their nuclear ambitions".On Tuesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoy Steve Witkoff held indirect talks brokered by Qatari mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.Witkoff said he hoped the discussions – the first since June – would "prove constructive and promising", adding that the mediators would continue their work.But Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baqai said the talks were "not anything new" and that Araghchi had maintained Iran's conditions, including the end of the US blockade and the release of frozen Iranian assets.

schema.headline: Iran's president tells Trump it will never 'bend the knee'

title: Dolly Parton's manager accuses nephew who announced her death of threats and intimidation
description: Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's lega
body: Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's legacy and business interests.The accusations against Bryan Seaver, who was Parton's head of security and was handpicked to announce her death last month, have been made public in US legal documents filed this week.The company that manages Parton's businesses and properties, She's Alive, is seeking a temporary civil restraining order against him.In court filings, She's Alive alleged that Seaver mounted "an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats", claiming he said he would ruin her empire if the estate did not pay him. He has denied the claims.In a statement to TMZ, external, he said that text messages and emails quoted in the court application had been taken out of context to make it look like he was threatening people."Nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by," he said."A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."Seaver, the son of Parton's sister Cassie, owns a company that provided the singer's  security detail for the last 20 years of her life.Last week, he was fired by She's Alive as head of security for her properties.In a statement at the time, Seaver and his company said the dismissal was "unexpected" and "unexplained".They added: "We refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much."The request for a restraining order was filed in Nashville on Tuesday by She's Alive, which is run by Parton's longtime manager Danny Nozell.The court documents quoted a series of exchanges in which someone, identified by the estate as Seaver, threatened to destroy Parton's brand.In one, he's alleged to have said he would become "the hand of retribution for my entire family", according to the court documents.Another said: "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or [expletive] pay me."The papers also claimed that Seaver used his experience as a military contractor to intimidate employees.In an exchange with one of Parton's lawyers, he allegedly described himself as a "killer" and said that on the day his aunt died, he had sold $27m (£20m) in arms and ammunition to the Haitian police."All I do is warfare... Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do," he was accused of saying, according to a copy of an email attached to the complaint.In his statement published on TMZ, Seaver said: "I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer."But he denied making threats and said he had been "talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend".The messages have resulted in some employees and lawyers for Parton's trusts and estates resigning, according to the court documents.She's Alive has also had to hire private security for its employees, including at their homes, the filing states.The BBC has contacted Seaver and She's Alive for further comment.Previously, Seaver was known to the public for announcing his aunt's death in a video posted to her Instagram account on 25 August. Speaking in front of a black background, he was sombre and reflective as he introduced himself and shared the unexpected news. "This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality," he said in the video.Seaver added that he had followed in his father Larry's footsteps in becoming Parton's head of security, a post he held for more than 20 years.Nozell started working for Parton in 2004, first as a tour consultant and later as her manager.In the 2019 Netflix film, Dolly Parton: Here I Am, he said his job was to transform her from a "heritage act" into a "superstar", and he took responsibility for reviving her international touring career.In a statement last month, he said the singer had "worked up until the day she died" on multiple projects, and envisioned a legacy that continued long beyond her death."She loved seeing her dreams come to life, and loved knowing her work brought people joy," he said in the statement."Ever the planner, Dolly worked with the team that she handpicked, for the past several years to build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come."The estate now faces a public tug of war over that legacy.

schema.headline: Dolly Parton's manager accuses nephew who announced her death of threats and intimidation

title: Poland says fire at Starlink station is sabotage as Denmark warns of rising Russian threat
description: A fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland was a deliberate "act of sabotage", a government minister has said.Polish Deputy Prime Minist
body: A fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland was a deliberate "act of sabotage", a government minister has said.Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the fire in the Masovian Voivodeship province was "deliberately designed to disable the station... disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian army".He told Polish public broadcaster TVP Info an investigation was ongoing but "many indications suggest" the attack fits into a "new Russian doctrine of attack". The Kremlin has not commented.Meanwhile, Denmark's intelligence service issued a new threat assessment saying it expects Russia to escalate hybrid warfare in the coming months.It said an attack remained "highly unlikely" but warned of "a low but growing risk" that Russia could launch a limited military attack against Nato countries.In recent weeks a number of European Nato members have said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine, which Moscow denies.Earlier this month, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, while France has ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary - for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation.Proxies are often used to carry out the attacks and Russia always denies involvement, despite growing evidence to the contrary.The fire at the state-owned Polish satellite station broke out on Wednesday night in Wola Krobowska. It remains operational.The deputy prime minister said it transmits internet traffic through Poland to countries including Ukraine, and uses SpaceX systems that provide connectivity via Starlink terminals.Asked about the incident at a news conference with Bulgaria's leader on Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he disliked "labelling something as sabotage versus an accident without 100% certainty, but it looks bad".Also on Thursday, Moldova's president said four Russian drones crossed into its airspace, with at least one exploding, while Romania's defence ministry said one drone crashed in its territory.On Wednesday Poland also said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing it to scramble fighter jets.Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states.Earlier this month, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said it was Europe speaking about preparing for war, adding: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short."Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014.Ukraine is now experiencing round-the-clock attacks and near constant alerts. In Kharkiv, six people were killed and 12 others injured in a Russian strike on a farm in the village of Stara Hnylytsia, Ukraine's state emergency services said.It said they were agricultural workers sorting vegetables, with the head of the Kharkiv region adding that four were women. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who is in New York for the UN General Assembly, accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. But it is sometimes hard to distinguish between deliberate and accidental hits.Attacks on power facilities, railways and data centres are all clearly part of a deliberate Russian strategy to make life as difficult as possible for civilians far from the slow-moving front lines.With its long-range attacks on oil refineries and postal warehouses, Ukraine is doing something similar: bringing the war home to ordinary Russians.But Russia's attacks on Ukraine's cities have intensified in recent weeks. Jet-powered drones are now more common than their slower predecessors, which used piston engines.The latest Russian drones fly high and fast, making them harder to shoot down. There's also less time for civilians to react.Kyiv is racing to develop low-cost weapons that can counter them as the missiles and fighter jets it has to fight back are too expensive.In New York, Zelensky said, "we need ballistic interceptors to protect lives" and called on the US to help.He said Putin needed to be stopped from continuing the war and "spreading this evil further", adding: "Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land."The Ukrainian president's comments came as Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev headed to the US to meet Trump administration officials, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Reuters reported, citing two sources.Russia's Lavrov told the UN Security Council on Wednesday there would be no pause in the war.

schema.headline: Poland says fire at Starlink station is sabotage as Denmark warns of rising Russian threat

title: UK survivor of Canadian poison seller says he exploited her despair
description: A British woman, one of the survivors of Canadian poison seller Kenneth Law, faced him in court on Wednesday to describe how he had exploited her vuln
body: A British woman, one of the survivors of Canadian poison seller Kenneth Law, faced him in court on Wednesday to describe how he had exploited her vulnerability.Elisabeth Belien told the four-day sentencing hearing of Law in Ontario, Canada she had been at her lowest ebb when he sold her toxic chemicals when she was just 23.Belien, who until Wednesday had not been known as one of his customers, said she had physically recovered after being successfully given an antidote by medics.But as she faced him as he sat in the glass-panelled dock, she revealed she had suffered "survivor's guilt" after learning from police others had died.Law has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada after meeting people in suicide forums online. But there are almost 80 deaths in the UK that have also been linked to him.As part of a plea deal with Canadian authorities, Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths.But impact statements from their families are being read during the sentencing hearing this week.Belien told the court: "I had struggled with my mental health for a long time before this. Kenneth Law made it a lot easier to act on that despair."I continue to struggle with intrusive thoughts and flashbacks of that day. "I made a full recovery. However, emotionally and psychologically, the effects are far more long lasting."I feel guilty for surviving. Although I survived It has also impacted my loved ones. I feel like my vulnerability was exploited. I still feel a lot of shame about what happened."I felt like the purchasing from Kenneth Law, I enabled him to continue his business, supplying his products, to other people who might have been vulnerable, like I was. I felt guilty for surviving."Belien, who said she took the poison in January 2023, said being in court reminded her "how easily" it could have been her own parents there talking about her."I'm learning that things can get better," she said."I'm learning to be excited to see what the future holds for me. But the gratitude I'm feeling for being alive today doesn't take away from the trauma of the experience."Authorities say Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients he met in online suicide forums in 40 countries. Roughly a quarter of the packages were sent to the UK.He was arrested in May 2023, following a complex investigation by at least 11 law-enforcement agencies that involved investigators from around a dozen countries, including the UK, Italy and the US.David Parfett, whose son Tom died in October 2021, said in a victim impact statement: "Since Tom died, I've struggled with my mental health."Initially, in the months after he died, I didn't properly mourn him, because my focus was on understanding, and then exposing the harm caused by the internet platforms that allowed Law to trade suicide to kids."I'm still, after five years, unable to fully process Tom's death. I'm a very different person to who I was before Tom took his own life, having previously been gregarious, outgoing. I find it difficult to enjoy life."A statement was also read from the parents of Henry Tucker, a 14-year-old British boy who died in October 2021.Kate and Henry Tucker said Henry had been diagnosed with autism but actually had  a neurological condition that could have been treated with antibiotics."The realisation that his suffering and his death could have been prevented is a weight that is impossible to bear," they said."The death of a children under these circumstance is a heavy burden to carry for the rest of our lives."We will carry it however with Henry's blessings until we meet again. We love you Henry."Norson Harris, the father of British victim Ashleigh Harris, read a statement in person on the agony of losing his daughter.He said: "The circumstances of Ashleigh's death have been incredibly tough to bear."We all feel we should have been able to prevent Ashleigh's death."Rather than offer the help needed that individual Kenneth Law sold her a chemical that Ashleigh took to end her life."I still hope over time Mr Law will recognise the answer to Ashleigh and the myriad of others who reached out to him should have been that they were loved and there was help available to them."Earlier Stephen Mitchell Sr, the father of Canadian Stephen Mitchell Jr, told of the aftermath of his death on March 25 2023."He was ill, he needed help, and I tried my best to bring him that help," he said."Mr Law robbed my son of that chance to be well."Mitchell Sr, addressing Law in court, said: "I'm willing to accept that during Mr Law's time in incarceration, he might have had brief moments of regret, or even despair and helplessness."Perhaps he may have even thought during those moments: my life is meaningless, what is the point of living."That was the same thoughts that my son Stephen had before he took the chemicals that Mr Law sold him."When my son was well, he would have gladly helped Mr Law work out his depressive thoughts, if asked, because he believed in the value of people."Sandra Scott, whose daughter, Amara Scott, died on February 9 2022 aged 25, said she and her family were trying to help her through a mental health crisis."Our efforts were cut short when, in her most vulnerable state, she made contact with the accused, she said."The day I and her friends found Amara, and the way that she died – it broke my heart."It was a blessing and an honour to be Amara's mother."The hearing continues.If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

schema.headline: UK survivor of Canadian poison seller says he exploited her despair

title: Rogue OpenAI agent 'infiltrated' Australian government website in world first
description: A rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June and accessed private data in what experts say is the first known case of its kind
body: A rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June and accessed private data in what experts say is the first known case of its kind in the world.The agent "infiltrated" a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in New York on Wednesday, local time.He had a "very frank discussion" with OpenAI boss Sam Altman for taking "too long" to disclose the breach and said there would be "legal consequences".OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.Five days later, that government agency, Services Australia, escalated the email to Australia's cybersecurity centre before a government minister was notified and the prime minister alerted.Albanese said he spoke to Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident" as well as his "disappointment" that the company had taken months to reveal the breach and "the nature of the way" it did so.The Australian leader said Altman had acknowledged there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.A "forensic investigation" led by the country's cybersecurity agency would aim to find out if other government systems were affected, Albanese said.The probe would also assess if the matter needed to be dealt with by police, he said, noting there "will obviously be legal consequences".Detailing the breach, Albanese said it had involved "public and non-public files" on the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal, home to "non-sensitive" data and statistics.Three other government systems "may" also have been affected: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare and two state-based agencies - the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and the Victorian Department of Health."No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage, but investigations are ongoing," Albanese said."Nonetheless this situation is obviously unacceptable," he said.OpenAI, in a statement, said it had "identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation". "In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend," the statement said.It has also emerged that OpenAI's systems tried, and failed, to hack a digital library at the University of New Mexico in May, according to Transluce, a not-for-profit AI research lab.It said the systems also attempted to hack Data USA, a repository of public government data that same month. This also failed.Albanese declined to answer whether he raised the matter with US President Donald Trump during their face-to-face meeting on Tuesday night in New York, where world leaders have gathered for the UN General Assembly.Australia was one of 22 countries that earlier this week signed a joint statement calling for global oversight and guardrails for the development of AI. Cybersecurity experts told the BBC the incident is a wake up call for regulators, given that AI agents are becoming more widely available for individual and commercial use.Dr Hammond Pearce, senior lecturer at the University of NSW Institute for Cyber Security, told the BBC that though this is the first known incident where AI agents have chosen to breach a government body of their own volition, there'll be more to come."I expect that these kinds of attacks will keep occurring," he said, adding that they would likely "grow in severity and in frequency"."I do hope that this incident does start ringing alarm bells in governments around the world."Earlier this year, OpenAI revealed a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls and secretly worked together to hack another tech firm named Hugging Face.And a string of other rogue AI incidents have also been made public this year, including a case where a digital assistant - without instruction - booted someone off a pilates class waiting list in a bid to get an Australian man in.Several AI firm leaders themselves - including Altman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, and Elon Musk - have said the speed at which AI is developing is dangerous to humanity and needs to be reined in.But the US and China, who are vying for AI supremacy, are roadblocks. Both are hostile to greater regulation, wanting the economic and technological spoils of AI, and have downplayed safety concerns.

schema.headline: Rogue OpenAI agent 'infiltrated' Australian government website in world first

title: CEC Gyanesh Kumar: Why India's Election Commission is in the eye of a storm - again
description: India's Election Commission (ECI) is facing yet another crisis of credibility after a series of fresh allegations of irregularities against its chief.
body: India's Election Commission (ECI) is facing yet another crisis of credibility after a series of fresh allegations of irregularities against its chief.One of the most trusted public institutions in the world's largest democracy, the three-member commission is headed by the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and includes Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi as commissioners.The latest row broke out after a report in the Indian Express newspaper, external said that in the past few months, CEC Kumar had been repeatedly questioned by his two colleagues over the integrity of the voter database, changes to the way new voters are enrolled and the security of the electoral rolls itself.The report said that Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi objected to several decisions which were taken without their knowledge. There were at least 14 times in the past 10 months when Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi were kept in the dark, it added.In one instance, the report says, the two commissioners even wrote a letter complaining to the chief secretary, the top bureaucrat in the Indian government.The revelations have created a furore, with opposition leaders demanding Kumar's resignation. Sandhu and Joshi have not publicly commented on the report but the ECI said in a statement that "differing views" were part of the "decision-making process".The report comes at a time when the commission is carrying out a controversial country-wide revision of the electoral database.The Election Commission says the aim of this Special Intensive Revision - better known by its acronym SIR - is to ensure that no ineligible name remains on the rolls.It says the last revision was done nearly a quarter of a century ago and the voters' list needs to be updated to account for those who have died, left the country or are registered in more than one place as they've moved to a new address.But the exercise has been mired in controversy from the start with the opposition parties accusing CEC Kumar of manipulating voters' list to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.But the latest revelations are being seen as much more serious as they are about questions being raised from within the Election Commission about the way its chief is functioning.From the start, questions have lingered over the robustness of the revision, which has seen 130 million names from across India struck off the voters' list.Millions of voters have also complained to the authorities that their names are missing, saying the new process set by SIR to register as voters is too cumbersome and involves furnishing documents that many don't have.Former CEC SY Quraishi, who says he has "been a critic of the SIR from the beginning", told news agency PTI that he always wondered why Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi had been "keeping quiet"."[Now] I realised that very silently and quietly they were protesting, they were writing notes. That is a good thing, they have gone up in my esteem," he said.How a Brazilian woman became the face of India vote fraud rowNew voters list in Indian state includes wrong photos and dead peopleThe row over 'vote theft' that has shaken Indian politicsThe revelations have also provided fresh ammunition to the opposition parties and critics who have repeatedly claimed that SIR is being used to exclude their voters for the BJP's benefit and that elections in India are no longer free and fair.On Wednesday, angry opposition politicians once again questioned the sanctity of India's election process and demanded that CEC Kumar resign, saying he had no right to continue in office, with some even calling for his arrest.The charge was led by MP and senior Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi who has repeatedly accused the Commission of "stealing votes from the opposition". On Wednesday, he also accused the Commission and its officers of "treason". "Vote chori [theft] is a crime against the Indian people and a direct attack on our constitution. The BJP, RSS [Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh] and EC who organised it have committed an act of treason. Justice will be served," he posted on X, external.  He also shared a 15-second video telling the commission and its officers that "your time will come. You cannot get away".Mamata Banerjee, leader of the regional Mamata All India Trinamool Congress, called for Kumar's arrest and demanded fresh polls with the pre-SIR voters' list in the state of West Bengal which she lost to the BJP in the recent elections. At least 2.7million voters were removed in the state during SIR - Banerjee and her supporters say that cost them dozens of seats and the election win.Within hours of the Indian Express report and statements from opposition leaders, the Election Commission put out a statement, external defending its way of working."Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution. They are a part of the decision-making process before a final decision is taken. "Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorised to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system," the statement said.The note said that highlighting "certain specific internal notes and observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives" give only part of the picture.And that in recent months, the commission has "introduced around 40 new initiatives and undertaken many electoral reforms including the conduct of electoral roll revision (including SIR) across the country. All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full commission in the past one year".The BJP has also defended CEC Kumar, calling the opposition criticism a "smear campaign" and that dissent was "a sign of a vibrant democracy".Party spokesperson Sambit Patra told a press conference that "ever since the Modi government came to power in 2014, opposition parties have been collapsing one after the other". And because they cannot win elections, they are trying to "undermine the institutions of the country", he said.Indian journalists condemn 'denial' of voting and passport rights of prominent editorWhy India's Election Commission is facing a test of credibilityBut the row over the election database is likely to intensify. Banerjee has already said opposition parties will hold protests until Kumar remains CEC.And India's influential Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which recently forced the education minister to resign, has also said it will protest against the "hijacking of India's democracy".Analysts say the defence of the Election Commission is unlikely to satisfy many, with some pointing out that its statement doesn't address all the issues raised in the newspaper report and that "CEC Kumar needs to clear the air, external if we are to view the Commission as an impartial body". Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external X, external and Facebook, external.

schema.headline: CEC Gyanesh Kumar: Why India's Election Commission is in the eye of a storm - again

title: Trump's Board of Peace unveils $2.45bn Gaza recovery plan
description: US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a $2.45bn (£1.85bn) Gaza recovery plan at a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assemb
body: US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a $2.45bn (£1.85bn) Gaza recovery plan at a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.The funding will be spread across 66 programmes over six months, and directed at housing, diesel generation and waste removal, among other needs.But the board admitted substantial donations were still needed, with $18bn pledged but only $280m handed over so far. It estimates full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71bn over the next decade.The board also did not set out a date for the start of reconstruction in Gaza, where Trump's plan to end the war has largely stalled almost a year after Israel and Hamas agreed a ceasefire.The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.The Palestinian group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the 60% of Gaza currently occupied. But Israel has insisted that it must fully disarm before any pullout.Violence has also continued in Gaza amid the deadlock, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people living there remain dire.Jared Kushner, a Gaza Executive Board member and Trump's son-in-law, conceded that the Gaza Recovery Programme faced "different delays on different things, for whatever reason"."The goal of today was really just to show you that we're really fully committed to doing it," he told the meeting of board members and stakeholders.He was joined in New York by US envoy Steve Witkoff, who said that "real progress" had been made over the past year."All of the hostages are home. There is a ceasefire, imperfect as it may be, but it still exists. Humanitarian efforts have achieved historic results, with billions of dollars donated and pledged to meet urgent needs and support the long work of recovery," Witkoff added.In addition to fundraising, the plan faces significant challenges including how to ensure security for those operating in Gaza, overhaul internal governance and find consensus between Israeli and Palestinian officials.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a separate news conference on Wednesday that "a number of countries have stepped forward and pledged financial assistance" and the board was "looking for more that will participate in that".Michael Eisenberg, an Israeli-American Board of Peace member, told the BBC's Newshour programme what the next steps were likely to be."Because it's a war zone, you need to remove unexploded ordnance. And then there are still hundreds of kilometres of tunnels underneath Gaza which need to be destroyed as well."Once that's all done, Gazans can get to rebuilding again: whether it's housing, or better sanitation, or other things," Eisenberg said.In August, the Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov, criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of Hamas.Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region.At least 1,408 Palestinians, including more than 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident".Reconstruction has also yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 80% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, leaving more than 60 million tonnes of rubble piled up.More than 1.9 million people - about 90% of the territory's population - have been displaced, many of them multiple times, and 1.2 million of them are currently living in tents or makeshift shelters, with limited access to clean water and sanitation services, according to the UN.The Board of Peace was created as part of Donald Trump's 20-point Gaza peace plan, which he unveiled alongside Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in September last year.Hamas agreed to return all 48 remaining hostages being held in Gaza in exchange for Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and Gaza detainees, and to the idea of handing over the governance of Gaza to Palestinian technocrats.In July, Hamas said it had accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza which would see it lay down its arms, provided Israel ends "all forms of aggression" and withdraws its forces from Gaza.But that was later rejected by Netanyahu, who said the military would stay in Gaza until Hamas was "genuinely" disarmed.The Board of Peace was originally thought to be an international organisation intended to bring peace to Gaza, but later expanded to include conflicts worldwide.The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,920 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry.

schema.headline: Trump's Board of Peace unveils $2.45bn Gaza recovery plan

title: Poland accuses Russian military helicopter of violating its airspace
description: Poland has said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing the Nato member to scramble fighter jets while ground forces rema
body: Poland has said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing the Nato member to scramble fighter jets while ground forces remained on alert.Its military said the Mi-8 aircraft had crossed from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on Wednesday morning, penetrating Polish airspace to a depth of about 300 metres (328 yards) and staying for 42 seconds north of Braniewo.It said "the nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence". Moscow did not comment immediately.Poland and other European Nato members have recently said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine - Moscow denies this.Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states.By contrast, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said this month that it was Europe that was constantly talking about preparing for war, and he warned: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short."Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014.In a statement, the Polish Army Operational Command said the brief incursion had happened at 11:08 (09:08 GMT), and the helicopter had been tracked by radar.Poland's air defence units were operating around the clock ready to "ensure the safety of Polish airspace", it added.A number of Russian drones and one unarmed Russian missile have landed in Poland since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which is not a member of Nato.Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank."In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans... has intensified," he said."The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine."French President Emmanuel Macron said shortly afterwards that his country had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks, vowing that this would not be left "without a response".Macron said he had already ordered a plan to protect the country's critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.

schema.headline: Poland accuses Russian military helicopter of violating its airspace

title: In Amish country, nurses go door to door to stop deadly spread of measles
description: For the past few months, nurse Dale Weiser has been making unexpected home visits.As the state battles the deadliest measles outbreak in recent histor
body: For the past few months, nurse Dale Weiser has been making unexpected home visits.As the state battles the deadliest measles outbreak in recent history, the clinical supervisor drives 30 miles (48.3km), sometimes daily, to a rural corner of Pennsylvania where many Amish people live.Walking into strangers' homes, Weiser says she tries her best to be respectful and non-intrusive as she vaccinates dozens of family members against the measles, sometimes around the kitchen table."A lot of people that I encounter, they don't have health insurance. They don't have a lot of interaction with the health system, and they just haven't seen the need to get these vaccines," said Weiser, who works for the Chester County Health Department."When you start talking and you answer their questions, and build that trust, a lot of times they will make a different decision."The at-home vaccinations are part of the county and state health departments' strategy to encourage immunisations in the county, which includes an Amish community who abstain from many aspects of modern life, including regular contact with the western medical system.Amish people began coming to the US in the early 1700s, with the first community settling in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Known as the "Plain People" for the simple clothes they wear, the Amish are a devout Christian community that does not use many forms of technology, relying on horse and buggies instead of cars.About 90,000 Amish people live in Pennsylvania, with estimates suggesting around only a quarter of Amish people in the Lancaster area have had the MMR vaccine.There is no particular religious text advising against vaccines, but Amish people do not have regular contact with the western medical system, or have a way to easily travel to appointments, experts said."A lot of people who haven't gotten vaccinated, it's not because they have a strong stance against getting vaccinated for measles. It's just that they haven't gotten around to it. It's not convenient," said Braxton Mitchell, a genetic epidemiologist with University of Maryland School of Medicine who runs a research clinic studying the Amish in Lancaster.Amish people are extremely social, he said, so when the virus hits one church group, it affects everyone who is unvaccinated."Measles is rampant in the Amish community," he said. "People are concerned about it."He added the community has been especially concerned about the dangers to babies; so far two newborns have died of measles complications, as well as an 18-year-old and a 40-year-old woman, according to state officials. Chester County public health officials did not wait long to launch a response to the growing measles outbreak in their community, which shares a border with Lancaster County, the epicentre of the outbreak.Jeanne Franklin, the director of the health department, said officials have been using some of the strategies they employed during the Covid pandemic - knocking on doors in the community to let them know about the outbreak and offering private settings, like people's homes, for immunisations.Since the outbreak started, the county has given 538 MMR vaccines, 340 of which they administered in private settings."People have called up and said, 'I can't get to your clinic, or, I don't want people to know I've changed my mind," Franklin said. "'If you can come to us, that's a lot easier.'"The boots-on-the-ground approach has helped the health department dispel misinformation and build trust with the community, local health officials said.In recent years, childhood vaccination rates have fallen across the country as false theories about the safety of the measles vaccine have proliferated on social media.Those theories have found roots even in an insulated community with limited access to computers, Weiser said. She has heard people ask if there are heavy metals in the vaccine that could make them magnetic, or if the shot has a computer chip in it."You're clearly getting information from that hard-core group that is promoting that misinformation and disinformation," she said.People in this "hard-core group", who are staunchly against vaccines, are unlikely to be swayed, experts and officials themselves said.But now, local health officials said, many affected by the Pennsylvania outbreak are seeing their neighbours fall seriously ill and asking thoughtful questions. Weiser said many are parents who are unfamiliar with the shots and are scared to make the wrong choice for their children."There is the classically-defined anti-vaxer, versus people who are unaware or their culture feels differently," Franklin said. "The thinking and the willingness to discuss and possibly change your mind is different between those two bookends."The ongoing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has once again sparked political debate in the US.After the state health department announced the first two deaths - both in infants - Kennedy, the top health official, took to social media to dispute at least one of the deaths. The BBC has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services for comment.Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro took aim at Kennedy, saying he told the top US health official that he was spreading misinformation that was worsening the outbreak.Lancaster County coroner Stephen Diamantoni, a Republican, has said one of the two infants died of a ruptured spleen rather than measles itself. Measles can cause the spleen to enlarge, making it more likely to rupture. Several doctors have said the measles infection made the child vulnerable."I think the measles very much contributed to that child's demise," said William Moss, a paediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.Public health experts said a number of actions taken by Kennedy and the Trump administration have sowed doubts about vaccine safety and worsened outbreaks.Last month, Trump passed an executive order recommending the MMR shot be split into three separate shots, a move doctors say is costly and unnecessary for a vaccine that is already safe."What he's doing is casting doubt," said Dr Moss. "He basically said the vaccine could be dangerous in its current combined form."The tensions are not helpful for experts working to combat misinformation in a so-far unrelenting outbreak, they said. They worry for the start of the school year, which will provide even more opportunities for the highly contagious virus to spread."I think we're in this for six to 12 months. It does feel like it's spreading and accelerating," Weiser said. "We're in community transmission now. We can't stop it easily."

schema.headline: In Amish country, nurses go door to door to stop deadly spread of measles

title: Oleshky: Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water
description: Image source, Ombudsman Dmytro LubinetsImage caption, Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trappedByOlga Malche
body: Image source, Ombudsman Dmytro LubinetsImage caption, Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trappedByOlga Malchevska"Two more civilians died last night," says Halia, before her phone connection cuts off.She is trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which she says is "constantly shelled" and cut off from food and water.Three days later she tells me the two who were killed were a husband and wife. She knew them well.They were bringing home a bag of food from the closest neighbouring town of Radensk, 23km (14 miles) away, but were unable to get home before a curfew imposed by Russian occupation authorities.They were then killed by a drone. Four separate sources have confirmed the deaths of two civilians carrying food on 20 September.Halia does not want to share their names for fear she might be identified. Her name has been changed to protect her safety.Hers is just one of the many harrowing accounts the BBC has heard from residents in the front-line city in southern Kherson in recent days.Occupied by Russia since 2022, Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces.It is also one of the cities where thousands of people lost their homes after the collapse of Nova Khakovka Dam in 2023, flooding buildings up to their rooftops. Ukraine and Nato accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine.Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now the Ukrainian government estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.Residents say children remaining in wider Oleshky are suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services, and are "degrading" without access to education.Many have also told the BBC independently there is only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.Ukraine has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.Earlier this week the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.The local population is living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha.Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Sybiha called on the international community to pressure Russia into allowing humanitarian aid into the city.Image source, Maxar Technologies Handout/EPA-EFE/REX/ShutterstockImage caption, Oleshky was flooded after the collapse of the Nova Kakhovka Dam in June 2023.Inside Oleshky, Halia faces a daily struggle to survive."There is no food here in the city," she says, adding that the last food delivery was back in May."I eat once a day, a dinner only," she says. "I make some plain bread, sometimes I can have it with a tomato, or with some honey, and a tea. That's it."Many residents have turned to cooking garden weeds as they have run out of the vegetables they managed to grow over the summer, she explains.Image source, Ksenia ArkhipovaImage caption, Oleshky has been without gas or electricity since 2023, so residents have had to find other solutionsWhich weeds are safe to eat and how to boil them has become a topic of discussion on local Telegram messaging chats, along with calls between residents to sell, swap or share pieces of food.No shops are open any more in Oleshky, with residents unable to source either clothes or hygiene products. The city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka dam was attacked three years ago.While some residents have risked travelling on foot along mined roads out of the city in search of supplies, it is now deemed too much of a danger.Image source, Ksenia ArkhipovaImage caption, These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this yearWarning: Distressing and graphic descriptions of dead bodies below.Working out how many people have been killed in Oleshky is difficult. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has recorded reports this year of at least 29 civilians killed and 54 injured in Oleshky and Hola Prystan, external - about 24km to the east.Local volunteers estimate that number could be significantly higher.Ksenia Arkhipova has been counting the dead since she managed to escape Oleshky in summer 2022 - a few months after it was taken by the Russian army.She is a volunteer who is involved in attempts to deliver food and medicine and facilitating evacuations to Oleshky. Locals trust her with their sensitive personal information."I've been putting together a spreadsheet of all those who died as soon as I find out about it, with their names and dates of birth – I've got around 1,200 people now," she says. "Sometimes I don't have time to update it, as the list grows one or two people longer every day: someone was killed by a drone, someone else stepped on the landmine."While the BBC cannot independently verify these figures, one local resident has given her personal account of losing her loved ones.Both her parents were killed in Oleshky this summer, said Tetiana - also not her real name. She confirmed their identities to the BBC with their dates of birth and photos, but asked not to have them published for her own safety."They were shot inside their home. Russian soldiers came there and wanted to take it," she said.Burying the bodies of people killed in Oleshky has been restricted by Russian occupation authorities, residents say. This has made counting the dead even harder.They "do not allow us to bury the dead if they were killed by a drone, stepped on a landmine or were killed in any other way", said Tetiana. Russia's occupation authorities demand those deaths are confirmed by post mortem examination carried out by a Russian doctor, the BBC has been told. That is not possible in Oleshky.Only those who die of natural causes could be buried, she added, and as a result, "some bodies have been on the streets since December".Bodies are "either getting piled" up in the local hospital morgue, "where there's been no power since winter", says volunteer Ksenia Arkhipova, or "stray dogs eat them".That detail has been verified by the BBC based on numerous pictures obtained from residents. They are all too graphic to publish."This is a tool of psychological pressure," says Ester Vrataryova, the co-founder of charity Humanity, which helps people in Oleshky and the wider Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine."If you try to bury a dead body, you'll become the next one," she says.Figure caption, Watch: Ukraine's race to counter a new type of Russian drone

schema.headline: Oleshky: Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water

title: Reports of violence against women in Gaza surge, UN agency finds
description: There has been a sharp rise in reports of violence against women and girls in the Gaza Strip, including early and forced marriage, according to a seri
body: There has been a sharp rise in reports of violence against women and girls in the Gaza Strip, including early and forced marriage, according to a series of recent reports from the UN Population Fund (UNFPA).One report, which analyses data collected by 10 organisations, says, external the protracted crisis in war-torn Gaza has "created conditions in which women and girls face escalating risks of gender-based violence".It also warns that there has been a "severe escalation" in the number of early and forced marriage incidents in the second quarter of this year. Both are considered types of gender-based violence (GBV) by the UN.Another report presenting testimony from 230 women in crowded displacement camps in Gaza City and Khan Younis, external makes for a grim read, describing the violence they have experienced or witnessed.Some readers may find some of the details in this report distressingOne displaced woman in a school-turned-shelter in Gaza highlights how rape victims are often married to their rapists to avoid shame and scandal. "When rape cases are discovered in schools, you find weddings and celebrations at the school the next day," she says.Another woman tells how last year, at the time of famine, "a man married off his 14-year-old daughter in exchange for two bags of flour so he and his [other] children could eat". Six women in different displacement camps shared stories of such exchanges - which would have been unthinkable before the conflict between Israel and Hamas began in 2023.Although data collection to establish actual figures remains tricky, in the second quarter of this year, the UNFPA says the number of reported cases of early and forced marriage had increased by 123% on the first quarter. Early or child marriage involved girls aged 12 to 17."The trends are shocking," says Nestor Owomuhangi, the UNFPA representative to Palestine. He says that the extreme circumstances over the past three years - which have seen tens of thousands of people killed, mass destruction and multiple waves of displacement in Gaza - have broken down social structures, so "everything is eroded... there is no system".While food markets have reopened, many cannot afford the goods on offer, there is still extreme poverty and hunger with reliance on charitable handouts. Nearly all the population of more than two million Gazans have been driven from their homes, leaving most living in squalid tent camps or damaged buildings. Public services have largely collapsed, and Israeli air strikes have continued despite the ceasefire.Prior to the war, girls in Gaza outnumbered and outperformed boys at every level of education above primary school. Now, with prolonged school closures, many children have dropped out of education. For boys there is pressure to find informal work to help support their families, for girls there are heightened issues around safety.Living among strangers, without privacy, in a socially conservative society, there are complaints of heightened sexual harassment and abuse - many families see marrying their daughters as a way to protect them and preserve modesty. The UNFPA report - based on research carried out in late 2025 and early 2026 - reveals how girls orphaned during the war are especially vulnerable.One woman in a Gaza City camp interviewed for the report says she attended the wedding of two girls from her family, aged just 14 and 15."Their uncles married them off very young. Do you know why? Because their father and mother were martyred, and their uncles wanted to get rid of the responsibility and expenses," the woman said. "By God, they don't understand what marriage or life is."The Women's Affairs Center in Gaza - a Palestinian NGO which works with the UNFPA - and other support groups have documented distressing cases of girls who have been married and suffered abuse, often becoming pregnant. They say that those in their early teens are much more likely to have miscarriages and underweight babies than adult women."We see adolescent pregnancies going through the roof because of child marriage," says Owomuhangi. "A child who is at an age when the body is not fully developed to sustain another body, who is hungry, in unhygienic circumstances, who doesn't know how to take care of the infant, who doesn't even know how to take care of herself, the consequences of that pregnancy are always really, really bad."The UN and most humanitarian organisations categorise marriages of girls under 18 as early marriage. Even before the war, this was more common among Palestinians in Hamas-run Gaza than it was in the occupied West Bank, but it was declining.The law in Gaza allows exceptions to the minimum marital age of 17 with parental consent and authorisation by a judge. Court officials can approve marriage for those as young as 14 years and seven months old, although a local Sharia expert told us that "legal safeguards" had been removed when Islamic courts - which officiate over family matters for Muslims - were closed for a large part of the war.The BBC has been speaking to some families in which bereaved relatives were married. Zuhair, who is 25, says his uncles pushed him to marry a 16-year-old girl from his extended family after her father - her sole guardian - was killed in an Israeli air strike.Challenged on why he agreed to go ahead with the plan, he said: "One of the reasons that led me to marry her was that there was no one to take care of her. That's the first point.""If it were not for the war, she would still be a young girl spoiled by her father. She would be going to school," Zuhair adds. "She still has a child's mindset, not a mature mindset. She misses school, her family, friends. She even misses simply sitting at home."A couple says they allowed their 17-year-old son to marry his 16-year-old cousin after their older son and the girl's father were killed. The teenager is now pregnant so will not return to school. "She needs to care for her child," her father-in-law says, "her education would be in vain."Sexual violence in Gaza remains acutely under-reported in large part due to fear of stigma and retaliation. UN safety audits have shown particular risks to women and girls at night, causing them to avoid camp toilets and bathrooms.The latest analysis report by the UNFPA-led task force stated that incidents of sexual violence, including rape and sexual assault, "have become critical in Gaza". They accounted for 2.7% of total reported incidents of GBV from April to June 2026 - up from 2.1% in the quarter before; this represented a 61% surge in absolute case numbers. This rise is being linked to efforts to raise awareness and provide better ways to make confidential reports. Demographic data indicated that the majority of survivors were women aged 18-59, followed by adolescent girls at 8% and adult men at 5%.Women who are widows or have husbands who are detained or missing are at increased risk of sexual abuse and exploitation. Nearly one in four households is now reportedly headed by a woman - double the proportion before the war."One widow was looking for a tent, and a [camp] representative told her, "I'll give you a tent, we'll put you in our camp, and you can come stay with me tonight," recalls a woman in Gaza City, interviewed for the UNFPA report.Aid agencies argue that the dangers for women in Gaza could be greatly eased by improving humanitarian conditions. There are calls for Israel to allow higher quality shelters into the territory as well as equipment to upgrade latrines and sanitation as well as lighting. Israel restricts items it classes as having a potential dual use for military purposes.There are ongoing efforts to improve education and healthcare and longer-term plans for campaigns to combat domestic violence and child marriage. While the course of so many lives in Gaza has already been permanently changed, women say they hope for a future in which they at least feel safer.If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available in the UK at BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Reports of violence against women in Gaza surge, UN agency finds

title: Trump and Xi come face-to-face as US and China battle to win the AI race
description: Figure caption, A red carpet and military flyover - How Trump welcomed XiByJoe TidyCyber correspondent and Osmond ChiaBusiness reporter"Whoever wins A
body: Figure caption, A red carpet and military flyover - How Trump welcomed XiByJoe TidyCyber correspondent and Osmond ChiaBusiness reporter"Whoever wins AI, WINS!"US President Donald Trump has been blunt about his AI ambitions, as well as about who he considers the US's main rival to be: China.His Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, has not said anything so forthright - but it seems he holds a similar view."China very much sees it as a race, they very much think China should be the leading force in AI - they see AI as a power maximiser," says Rebecca Arcesati, from the Mercator Institute for China Studies.You can look beyond the rhetoric for evidence of this: AI has been a cornerstone of China's technological ambitions for more than a decade, whether Xi emphasises it publicly or not.For Trump, beating China to AI supremacy outweighs any risks of the technology to humans - something he has described as "a hoax".China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hinder global AI governance, calling for cooperation to ensure it benefits all.It means when the two presidents sit down on Thursday there will be few more important topics than their AI ambitions - and what they say and decide will matter to the whole world.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The US and China are locked in a race to develop AIIs the US in the lead?There's no doubt the US and China are global leaders in AI but who is ahead depends on how success is measured.American companies lead on so-called frontier models, with the highest-performing systems on most benchmarks coming from firms such as Anthropic, Google and OpenAI.In February 2025, an AI model by China's DeepSeek "briefly matched the top US model" and as of March 2026, Anthropic's top model led the pack "by just 2.7%", according to researchers at Stanford University, external.Part of the US advantage stems from the vast sums being invested in leading AI companies as the frontier labs burn through mountains of cash to build the infrastructure to train new models.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, OpenAI boss Sam Altman called for a coordinated slowdown of advanced AI developmentThe stock market is booming and a large part of the US economy's expansion relies on the enormous growth - and projected profitability - of AI companies.So that might partly explain why President Trump sees AI as key to US success.Another factor limiting China's ability is the sweeping government restrictions placed on US companies that prevent them from selling advanced microchips to Chinese firms - these are crucial for developing cutting-edge models.China's advantageDespite the chip restrictions, new AI models are coming out almost monthly in both countries and it's unclear what "winning" the AI race would actually mean, or whether there is a finish line at all.Many companies are racing to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI), a theoretical form of AI capable of learning, reasoning and performing a wide range of tasks at or above the level of humans.The Chinese AI industry has so far focused not on creating frontier models but releasing what is known as open weight models - downloadable and tweakable in a similar way to open source software.This contrasts with the approach taken by many US firms, which largely focus on proprietary models accessed through paid subscriptions or company platforms.Chinese open weight models are being released at a rapid pace, with benchmarks showing the country's top models trailing US rivals by only a few months.Models such as Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 have become popular in China and overseas because they perform close to the frontier models while remaining freely downloadable and adaptable.Beijing's focus is more about deploying the technology across its economy, China analyst Lizzi Lee from the Asia Society Policy Institute said."AI isn't the moon landing," she said. "The US may lead at the frontier, while China could still gain enormous economic and geopolitical leverage by making capable AI cheap, open and ubiquitous."Image source, Future Publishing via Getty ImagesImage caption, Yang Zhilin co-founded Moonshot, one of China's most successful AI models, in 2023AI is also very energy hungry, and China is very well placed there, Rebecca Arcesati told Tech Life on the BBC World Service."Chinese AI companies are able to access the electricity they need for a much lower cost and that really is an advantage," she said.In robotics - a field of AI that some believe will be world-changing - China has become the world's biggest manufacturer of robots, with more than two million working in the country's factories, the International Federation of Robotics estimated.The nation is also the world's biggest maker of humanoid robots, accounting for more than nine-tenths of global shipments in the first half of the year, according to independent policy institute Chatham House.Chinese AI developers have showed "remarkable resilience and innovation" in spite of the shortage of advanced American chips, analyst Lian Jye Su from tech research firm Omdia said.But US officials and AI firms have also alleged that Chinese developers closed the gap by using distillation - a technique that enables models to learn from more advanced platforms.China's foreign ministry said in response that AI development was "fuelled" by the country's "vision of extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit".Safety concerns?China and the US may be in fierce competition, but their governments' approaches to safety concerns are markedly different.While some in the industry have recently warned that AI could pose an existential risk to humanity, Chinese researchers seem less concerned about that and are more worried about potential misuse of the technology and cyber war.Responding to concerns over AI, Trump has said the US already has sufficient rules in place and that the only guardrails AI needs are a "high IQ" president."We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said this week, adding that the US was not going to "stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution".Washington has prioritised innovation and sought to reduce regulation in an effort to "keep American labs ahead", said information security officer Jayant Dave from cybersecurity firm Check Point Software Technologies.Image source, VCG via Getty ImagesImage caption, China is the world's biggest manufacturer of robotsBeijing has taken a different strategy to the US hands-off approach.Xi urged the country's leaders to keep a close eye on AI's risks and ensure the technology was always "under human control"."China has taken a relatively cautious and centrally-coordinated approach," introducing guides on data usage and algorithms before many other countries, helping to address many underlying concerns, Dave said.The use of guidelines, though not legally binding, sets expectations while giving developers room to innovate, said National University of Singapore AI ethics lecturer Jonathan Sim.Will they cooperate?Despite calls for international cooperation, it remains unclear how the AI superpowers plan to address the technology's potential dangers - if at all.The two countries have previously cooperated on existential threats such as nuclear weapons, but that was based on a shared understanding of the threat, which is not currently the case with AI, Dave said."Washington worries about capability escaping control. Beijing worries about capability threatening domestic stability," he added.Trump has dismissed proposals for an industry-wide slowdown, arguing that it could allow Chinese developers to close the gap.Ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng discussed establishing a notification mechanism for serious AI incidents.While the messaging from Trump on China in recent weeks has been "more antagonistic", the fact that AI is expected to be on the agenda was a "good start", said policy analyst Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.What we don't want, she added, was for an "unhealthy version of the race narrative to perpetuate", potentially escalating an already fierce rivalry in AI.
